title: The game, made exact
sub: A one-dimensional GAN, with the discriminator played perfectly.

frames.caption: Real data (grey) has two clusters. The generator (orange) starts as a narrow blob in the middle. Blue is the best possible discriminator for this generator, D* = p<sub>data</sub> / (p<sub>data</sub> + p<sub>G</sub>): near 1 where only real data lives, near 0 where only fakes do.
The generator follows the discriminator: its mass is pushed out of the regions D* calls fake and towards the ones it calls real.
Half of the generator has found the left cluster. The other half has spread wide to reach the right one, so it is now too dense in the gap between them, and D* dips well below ½ there.
The wide half drifts right only slowly: the signal from D* is weak here. Uneven progress like this is typical of GAN training.
It narrows onto the second cluster. D* is flattening: each point is getting harder to call.

p<sub>G</sub> = p<sub>data</sub>, and D* = ½ everywhere: the best discriminator can do no better than a coin flip. This is the equilibrium, and the generator's loss has reached its minimum, −log 4 ≈ −1.386.

Real data is uniform on [0, 1] and the generator's samples are uniform on [θ, θ + 1], starting at θ = 3: they don't overlap at all. Blue is the Jensen-Shannon divergence as a function of θ, orange is the earth mover's distance W₁.

Move the generator from θ = 3 to 2. W₁ falls from 3 to 2: it knows the generator got closer. JSD stays at log 2 ≈ 0.69. Its slope, and so the gradient a standard GAN's generator receives, is exactly zero.
Still no overlap, still a flat JSD: it equals log 2 · min(|θ|, 1). In high dimensions, where real images and early fakes live on thin, almost surely disjoint sets, this is the normal situation.
Only once the two overlap does JSD start to fall.
At θ = 0 both distances are zero. W₁'s slope is ±1 everywhere else, so gradient descent on it always knows which way to move the generator. That is the case for the Wasserstein GAN.
